newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai economic data paint mixed picture.
newsitem.headline: Thai economic data paint mixed picture.

text.p: The Bank of Thailand on Thursday released monthly economic data that showed a welcome smaller current account deficit but signalled that the country's sluggish exports remained weak.

Central bank chief economist Kleo-thong Hetrakul told reporters the current account deficit narrowed to 29.3 billion baht ($1.16 billion) in August from 31.0 billion in July and from a peak of 49.6 billion in April.

She attributed the smaller deficit to a bigger August service account surplus of 7.5 billion baht, a six-month high, against 4.5 billion in July, as the tourism industry earned more foreign exchange during the month.
However, private analysts expect the overall 1996 current account deficit to exceed the 1995 level of 8.1 percent of gross domestic product.
August's improved current account performance was in line with market expectations but was not matched by trade figures, with exports failing to show any signs of a pick-up.
Kleo-thong said August exports fell 117.7 billion baht from 121.7 billion a year ago, the third decline in three months, while imports contracted to 154.5 billion baht from 157.9 billion a year ago.
Chatchai Saelee of Chao Phaya Finance and Securities had forecast ahead of the central bank announcement that August exports would show a rise of three or four percent year-on-year.
Caretaker deputy prime minister Amnuay Viravan said on Tuesday that exports had risen a meagre 3.1 percent during the first eight months against some 25 percent a year ago.
Kleo-thong said the August trade deficit widened to 36.8 billion baht from 35.5 billion in July. Analysts earlier had expected a slightly smaller deficit in August.

Chatchai voiced a concensus among private economists that total 1996 exports would rise only five to six percent over 1995 against a 10.2 percent increase earlier projected by the central bank for this year and actual 23.6 percent growth in 1995.

Nuchjarin Kasemsukworarat of Dhana Siam Finance and Securities said the domestic economic slowdown continued in August with the private investment index posting lower year-on-year growth for the eighth month running.
The central bank said August private investment growth eased to 8.0 percent year-on-year, less than half of that for the same month a year ago when it surged 16.7 percent.
But Nuchjarin said: "Eight percent investment growth could hardly be viewed as a sign of recession. By any standard, it is quite moderate."

The analyst said private business tapped more baht loans from commercial banks for the second month in September after the central bank moved to curb corporate borrowing of short-term foreign funds a few months ago.

The central bank said outstanding commercial bank loans, excluding those extended through offshore banking units, rose 15.8 percent year-on-year in September against 15.0 in August, but compared with 22.7 percent a year ago.
